'''''Neltuma alba''''' (formerly ''Prosopis alba'') is a [[South America]]n tree species that grows in central [[Argentina]], the [[Gran Chaco]] ecoregion, and part of the [[Mesopotamia, Argentina|Argentine Mesopotamia]], as well as [[Bolivia]], [[Chile]], [[Paraguay]], and [[Peru]].<ref name=iucn/><ref name = powo/><ref>{{cite WFO|id=wfo-1000040065
|title=''Neltuma alba'' (Griseb.) C.E.Hughes & G.P.Lewis|access-date=13 February 2025}}</ref> It is known as ''algarrobo blanco'' ('white carob tree' or "white algarrobo") in [[Spanish language|Spanish]]. Spanish settlers gave it that name because of its similarity to the European [[Ceratonia siliqua|carob tree]] (''Ceratonia siliqua''). Other common names come from [[Guarani language|Guaraní]], including '''''ibopé''''' and '''''igopé'''''.

''Neltuma alba'' is a medium-sized tree, measuring between {{convert|5|and|15|m|ft|abbr=on|lk=on}}, in height and {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} in diameter, though such tall specimens occur very rarely at present. The trunk is short and the treetop is globular, sometimes reaching {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} in diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is thin, brown-grayish in colour, with streaks, and it has [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]] properties.

The tree is employed for ornamental and utilitary roadside planting and [[windbreak]]s. Its [[timber]], which is rather dense ([[relative density]] = 0.76) and difficult to work, is used for doors and floors, for furniture, for paving blocks, shoe lasts and [[Oak (wine)|wine casks]] (where it replaces the European [[oak]]). The wood responds well to drying and is therefore valuable for work that requires stable dimensions regardless of humidity. It is also durable for outdoor use.

The [[flower]]s are small, greenish-white or yellowish, and [[Plant sexuality|bisexual]].  [[Pollination]], mediated by [[Anemophily|wind]] and insects, is [[Allogamy|allogamous]] (crossed), since the female reproductive organs are turned active before the male ones.

The [[fruit]]s are modified [[Legume|seedpods]], {{convert|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, with brown [[seed]]s about {{convert|7|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.  They contain a sweet [[flour]]y paste (''patay''), very high in energy, that can be used for [[fodder]] or turned into [[flour]] for human consumption. In the 1940s a mildly intoxicating beverage called ''aloja'' was made from it through [[fermentation (food)|fermentation]]; in turn it was sometimes [[distillation|distilled]] to produce [[ethanol]]. Between half and three quarters of the fruit's weight is [[sugar]].

[[File:Yanbut.jpg|thumb|left|In a [[Botanical garden]] in [[Israel]]]]

The tree can reportedly tolerate [[drought]], salt and sand; in fact, it is extremely efficient with regard to water consumption, it produces the most fruits in years of drought and has been successfully introduced in arid terrains. However, it cannot stand even mild frost.

''Neltuma alba'' and other ''algarrobo'' species in genus ''[[Prosopis]]'', such as ''algarrobo negro'' (''[[Prosopis nigra|P. nigra]]''), are often confused or not correctly distinguished in botanical literature; in part this is due to the ease of [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] of the genus.

Two varieties are accepted:<ref name = powo/>
*''Neltuma alba'' var. ''alba'' (synonyms ''Prosopis atacamensis'' {{small|Phil.}} and ''Prosopis siliquastrum'' var. ''longisiliqua'' {{small|Phil.}}) – northern Argentina, Bolivia, northern Chile, Paraguay, and Peru
*''Neltuma alba'' var. ''panta'' {{small|(Griseb.) C.E.Hughes & G.P.Lewis}} (synonyms ''Prosopis alba'' var. ''panta'' {{small|Griseb.}} and ''Prosopis panta'' {{small|(Griseb.) Hieron.}}) – northern Argentina, Paraguay, and Peru
